topics.name: Kinetic Theory Postulates and the Ideal Gas Equation
topics.summary: Kinetic theory models a gas as a very large number of tiny molecules in continuous, random motion. The postulates are simple: molecules are point-sized compared with the spaces between them, they exert no forces on each other except during collisions, and every collision (with another molecule or with a wall) is perfectly elastic. From this picture the ideal gas equation follows. For \( \mu \) moles, \( PV=\mu RT \); written for \( N \) molecules it becomes \( PV=Nk_BT \), because \( R=N_Ak_B \). Dividing by volume gives \( P=nk_BT \), where \( n=N/V \) is the number density. Always use absolute temperature in kelvin. The same equation contains Boyle's law (fixed \( T \)), Charles's law (fixed \( P \)) and Avogadro's hypothesis: equal volumes of all gases at the same \( T \) and \( P \) hold the same number of molecules. Dalton's law of partial pressures follows too, since each gas in a mixture contributes \( n_ik_BT \). Note that molecular mass never appears in \( P=nk_BT \): heavy and light molecules at the same temperature and number density exert the same pressure.
topics.worked_example:
How many molecules per m\( ^3 \) are there at \( 1.38\times10^{5} \) Pa and 300 K? (\( k_B=1.38\times10^{-23} \) J/K)

\( n=\dfrac{P}{k_BT}=\dfrac{1.38\times10^{5}}{1.38\times10^{-23}\times300}=\dfrac{10^{28}}{300}\approx3.3\times10^{25} \) m\( ^{-3} \).
common_mistakes: Pairing \( R \) with a molecule count, or \( k_B \) with a number of moles
Using temperature in degrees Celsius instead of kelvin
Confusing the total molecule count \( N \) with the number density \( n \)
Thinking heavier molecules exert more pressure at the same \( n \) and \( T \)

topics.name: Pressure of an Ideal Gas and the Kinetic Interpretation of Temperature
topics.summary: Pressure arises because molecules bounce off the container walls and each bounce transfers momentum. Summing over all molecules gives \( P=\dfrac13nm\overline{v^2}=\dfrac13\rho\overline{v^2} \). The factor \( \dfrac13 \) appears because only one of the three perpendicular velocity components pushes on a given wall, and on average \( \overline{v_x^2}=\dfrac13\overline{v^2} \); it has nothing to do with the \( \dfrac12 \) in kinetic energy. Writing \( \bar E=\dfrac12m\overline{v^2} \) turns this into \( P=\dfrac23n\bar E \), or \( PV=\dfrac23E \) for the whole gas. Comparing with \( P=nk_BT \) gives the kinetic interpretation of temperature: \( \bar E=\dfrac32k_BT \). The average translational kinetic energy per molecule depends only on absolute temperature, not on the kind of gas, its pressure, or its volume. For one mole, the translational energy is \( \dfrac32RT \). At the same temperature a helium atom and an oxygen molecule have the same average translational energy, even though their speeds differ. Absolute zero is where this translational energy would vanish. Because \( \bar E \) is fixed by temperature, doubling the absolute temperature doubles the average kinetic energy of every molecule, whatever the gas; changing the pressure alone at constant temperature leaves it unchanged.
topics.worked_example:
Find the average translational kinetic energy of a molecule at 300 K. (\( k_B=1.38\times10^{-23} \) J/K)

\( \bar E=\dfrac32k_BT=\dfrac32\times1.38\times10^{-23}\times300=6.21\times10^{-21} \) J.
common_mistakes: Replacing \( \dfrac13 \) in the pressure formula by \( \dfrac12 \), or dropping it
Using \( N \) where the number density \( n \) is needed
Believing lighter molecules have more kinetic energy at the same temperature
Linking kinetic energy to pressure instead of temperature

topics.name: RMS Speed, Average Speed, and Most Probable Speed of Gas Molecules
topics.summary: Molecules of a gas move with a spread of speeds described by the Maxwell distribution, and three speeds summarise it. The rms speed is \( v_{rms}=\sqrt{\dfrac{3RT}{M}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{3k_BT}{m}} \); the average speed is \( v_{avg}=\sqrt{\dfrac{8RT}{\pi M}} \); the most probable speed, at the peak of the curve, is \( v_{mp}=\sqrt{\dfrac{2RT}{M}} \). The coefficients are 3, \( \dfrac8\pi \) (about 2.55) and 2, so the order is always \( v_{mp}<v_{avg}<v_{rms} \). Use \( R \) with molar mass \( M \) in kg/mol, or \( k_B \) with molecular mass \( m \) in kg; never mix the pairs. All three speeds grow as \( \sqrt T \) and fall as \( \dfrac{1}{\sqrt M} \), so at equal temperature hydrogen molecules move 4 times faster than oxygen molecules, since \( \dfrac{32}{2}=16 \). On heating, the Maxwell curve flattens and broadens, and its peak shifts to higher speed while the area under it stays fixed. The rms speed is the one tied to kinetic energy: \( \bar E=\dfrac12mv_{rms}^2 \). A useful shortcut is \( v_{rms}=\sqrt{\dfrac{3P}{\rho}} \), which needs only pressure and density. Remember that the speeds depend on temperature and molar mass alone, not on pressure by itself or on the size of the molecules.
topics.worked_example:
Find \( v_{rms} \) for oxygen (\( M=32 \) g/mol) at 320 K, with \( R=8.3 \) J/(mol K).

\( v_{rms}=\sqrt{\dfrac{3\times8.3\times320}{0.032}}=\sqrt{249000}\approx499 \) m/s, roughly 500 m/s. The other two speeds are smaller: \( v_{mp}
common_mistakes: Swapping the coefficients 2, \( \dfrac8\pi \) and 3 between the named speeds
Writing the order as \( v_{rms}<v_{avg}<v_{mp} \)
Plugging molar mass \( M \) into the \( k_B \) formula, or \( m \) into the \( R \) formula
Leaving \( M \) in g/mol
Forgetting the square root when scaling with \( T \) or \( M \)

topics.name: Degrees of Freedom and the Law of Equipartition of Energy
topics.summary: The degrees of freedom \( f \) of a molecule count the independent squared terms in its energy. A monatomic molecule has 3, all translational. A rigid diatomic molecule adds 2 rotations about axes perpendicular to its bond, giving \( f=5 \). A rigid non-linear polyatomic molecule can rotate about 3 axes, giving \( f=6 \). At high temperature a diatomic molecule can also vibrate, and one vibrational mode adds 2 degrees of freedom, one for vibrational kinetic energy and one for vibrational potential energy, so \( f=7 \). The law of equipartition states that in thermal equilibrium each degree of freedom carries on average \( \dfrac12k_BT \) per molecule. Hence the average energy per molecule is \( \dfrac f2k_BT \), and the internal energy per mole is \( U=\dfrac f2RT \). Translation always gets exactly \( \dfrac32k_BT \), whatever the molecule, so extra modes add energy without changing molecular speeds. For a gas at pressure \( P \) and volume \( V \), \( U=\dfrac f2PV \), because \( \mu RT=PV \). Mixtures are handled by adding each component's energy.
key_formulas: Monatomic \( f=3 \); rigid diatomic \( f=5 \); vibrating diatomic (high temperature) \( f=7 \); rigid non-linear polyatomic \( f=6 \)
topics.worked_example:
Find the internal energy of 2 mol of rigid nitrogen at 300 K, with \( R=8.3 \) J/(mol K).

\( f=5 \), so \( U=\dfrac52\mu RT=\dfrac52\times2\times8.3\times300=12450 \) J.
common_mistakes: Counting a vibrational mode as 1 degree of freedom instead of 2
Applying the monatomic \( f=3 \) to a diatomic gas
Giving a linear molecule 3 rotations
Thinking extra degrees of freedom raise translational energy or speed

topics.name: Specific Heat Capacities of Gases and Mean Free Path
topics.summary: Equipartition predicts molar heat capacities directly. At constant volume all heat raises internal energy, so \( C_v=\dfrac f2R \). At constant pressure the gas also does work \( R \) per mole per kelvin, so \( C_p=C_v+R \) (Mayer's relation), and \( \gamma=\dfrac{C_p}{C_v}=1+\dfrac2f \). This gives \( \gamma=\dfrac53 \) for monatomic, \( \dfrac75 \) for rigid diatomic, \( \dfrac97 \) for vibrating diatomic, and \( \dfrac43 \) for rigid non-linear polyatomic gases. The mean free path \( \lambda \) is the average distance a molecule travels between collisions: \( \lambda=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2\,\pi d^2n} \), where \( d \) is the molecular diameter and \( n \) the number density. The \( \sqrt2 \) accounts for the relative motion of the colliding molecules. Since \( n=\dfrac{P}{k_BT} \), \( \lambda \) decreases as pressure rises at fixed temperature, and increases with temperature at fixed pressure. In a sealed rigid container, \( n \) is fixed, so \( \lambda \) does not change on heating. The time between collisions is \( \dfrac{\lambda}{v_{avg}} \), and the collision frequency is its reciprocal. Doubling the molecular diameter cuts \( \lambda \) to one-fourth, because the effective collision area \( \pi d^2 \) grows fourfold.
topics.worked_example:
Find \( \lambda \) for \( d=3\times10^{-10} \) m and \( n=2.5\times10^{25} \) m\( ^{-3} \), with \( \sqrt2\,\pi\approx4.44 \).

\( \sqrt2\,\pi d^2n\approx4.44\times9\times10^{-20}\times2.5\times10^{25}\approx10^{7} \) m\( ^{-1} \), so \( \lambda\approx10^{-7} \) m.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to add \( R \) to \( C_v \) to get \( C_p \)
Dropping the \( \sqrt2 \) from the mean free path
Claiming \( \lambda \) increases with pressure
Using \( d \) instead of \( d^2 \)
Using a vibrating-diatomic value with vibration counted as 1 degree of freedom

questions.topic: Kinetic Theory Postulates and the Ideal Gas Equation
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an assumption of the kinetic theory of an ideal gas?
options: Gas molecules attract one another strongly at all separations
Gas molecules are in continuous, random motion
Collisions between gas molecules are perfectly elastic
The size of a molecule is negligible compared with the average distance between molecules
questions.explanation:
Kinetic theory assumes molecules exert negligible forces on each other except during collisions.

A strong attraction at all separations directly contradicts this, so it is not an assumption.

Random motion, elastic collisions and negligible molecular size are all standard postulates.
questions.hint: Recall what kinetic theory says about forces between molecules when they are not colliding.
distractor_logic: Random motion is a genuine postulate; molecules move in all directions with a range of speeds
Perfectly elastic collisions are a genuine postulate; no kinetic energy is lost in collisions
Point-sized molecules is a genuine postulate; molecular volume is ignored

questions.topic: Kinetic Theory Postulates and the Ideal Gas Equation
questions.question: In the kinetic theory of gases, collisions of molecules with each other and with the walls are assumed to be
options: partially elastic, with a small loss of kinetic energy in each collision
elastic with the walls but inelastic between molecules
questions.explanation:
Kinetic theory assumes every collision conserves total kinetic energy, i.e. it is perfectly elastic.

If energy were lost in collisions, an isolated gas would keep cooling, contradicting the steady temperature of a gas at equilibrium.
questions.hint: An isolated gas at equilibrium keeps a steady temperature. What does that say about energy lost in collisions?
distractor_logic: Perfectly inelastic collisions would make molecules stick together, which a gas does not show
A steady loss of kinetic energy would make an isolated gas cool on its own, which does not happen at equilibrium
The postulate treats all collisions alike; no distinction is made between wall and molecule collisions

questions.topic: Kinetic Theory Postulates and the Ideal Gas Equation
questions.question: For \( \mu \) moles of an ideal gas at pressure \( P \), volume \( V \) and absolute temperature \( T \), the ideal gas equation is
questions.explanation:
The ideal gas equation combines Boyle's, Charles's and Avogadro's laws: \( PV \) is proportional to both the amount of gas and the absolute temperature.

With the universal gas constant \( R \) as the constant of proportionality, \( PV=\mu RT \).
questions.hint: \( PV \) should increase if you add more gas or raise the temperature.
distractor_logic: Places \( T \) in the denominator; \( PV \) actually grows with temperature
Divides by the number of moles; more gas at the same \( T \) and \( V \) gives more pressure, not less
Multiplies by \( V \) instead of dividing; at fixed amount and \( T \), \( P \) falls as \( V \) rises

questions.topic: Kinetic Theory Postulates and the Ideal Gas Equation
questions.question: In terms of the total number of molecules \( N \), the ideal gas equation is written as
questions.explanation:
Since \( \mu=\dfrac{N}{N_A} \) and \( R=N_Ak_B \), \( PV=\mu RT=\dfrac{N}{N_A}N_Ak_BT \).

So \( PV=Nk_BT \): Boltzmann's constant \( k_B \) is the gas constant per molecule.
questions.hint: Replace the number of moles by \( N \) divided by Avogadro's number and see what \( R \) becomes.
distractor_logic: Pairs the molar constant \( R \) with a molecule count; \( R \) belongs with moles, \( k_B \) with molecules
Puts \( T \) in the denominator; \( PV \) must rise with temperature
Divides by \( N \); more molecules in the same volume at the same \( T \) must raise the pressure

questions.topic: Kinetic Theory Postulates and the Ideal Gas Equation
questions.question: The universal gas constant \( R \), Boltzmann's constant \( k_B \) and Avogadro's number \( N_A \) are related by
questions.explanation:
\( R \) is the gas constant for one mole; \( k_B \) is the same constant for one molecule.

A mole contains \( N_A \) molecules, so \( R=N_Ak_B \). Numerically, \( 6.02\times10^{23}\times1.38\times10^{-23}\approx8.31 \) J/(mol K).
questions.hint: One mole contains Avogadro's number of molecules.
distractor_logic: Inverts the relation; \( k_B \) is the constant for one molecule, so it is far smaller than \( R \)
Divides where it should multiply; \( R \) refers to a whole mole, which contains \( N_A \) molecules
Treats the per-mole and per-molecule constants as identical, ignoring the factor \( N_A \)

questions.topic: Kinetic Theory Postulates and the Ideal Gas Equation
questions.question: 2 mol of an ideal gas occupy \( 8.3\times10^{-3} \) m\( ^3 \) at 300 K. Taking \( R=8.3 \) J/(mol K), the pressure of the gas is
questions.explanation:
\( P=\dfrac{\mu RT}{V} \).

\( \mu RT=2\times8.3\times300=4980 \) J.

\( P=\dfrac{4980}{8.3\times10^{-3}}=6\times10^{5} \) Pa.
questions.hint: Rearrange \( PV=\mu RT \) for \( P \) and keep track of the power of ten in \( V \).
distractor_logic: Uses 1 mol instead of 2 mol, halving the result
Divides by the number of moles instead of multiplying, using \( P=\dfrac{RT}{\mu V} \)
Drops the power of ten in the volume, treating it as 8.3 m\( ^3 \)

questions.topic: Kinetic Theory Postulates and the Ideal Gas Equation
questions.question: A fixed amount of ideal gas is compressed to half its volume while its temperature is kept constant. Its pressure
questions.explanation:
At constant \( T \) and fixed amount, \( PV=\mu RT \) is constant (Boyle's law).

If \( V \) becomes \( \dfrac V2 \), \( P \) must become \( 2P \) to keep \( PV \) unchanged.

Kinetically, the same molecules now hit a smaller wall area more often.
questions.hint: What stays constant for a fixed amount of gas at constant temperature?
distractor_logic: Reverses Boyle's law; at constant \( T \), \( P \) and \( V \) are inversely related
Squares the volume ratio; \( P \) varies as \( \dfrac1V \), not \( \dfrac{1}{V^2} \)
Ignores that \( PV \) is constant at fixed \( T \); halving \( V \) must change \( P \)

questions.topic: Kinetic Theory Postulates and the Ideal Gas Equation
questions.question: According to kinetic theory, between two successive collisions a gas molecule moves
options: along a curved path, pulled by neighbouring molecules
with steadily decreasing speed until the next collision
in a small circle about a fixed point
in a straight line with constant velocity
questions.explanation:
Kinetic theory neglects intermolecular forces except during collisions.

With no net force, Newton's first law says the molecule moves in a straight line at constant velocity until it next collides.
questions.hint: What does Newton's first law say about a body with no net force on it?
distractor_logic: Curved paths would need intermolecular forces between collisions, which the theory neglects
Slowing down would need a force acting between collisions; with no force, speed stays constant
Circular motion needs a centripetal force; a free molecule has none

questions.topic: Pressure of an Ideal Gas and the Kinetic Interpretation of Temperature
questions.question: According to kinetic theory, the pressure of an ideal gas of density \( \rho \) and mean square speed \( \overline{v^2} \) is
questions.explanation:
Momentum delivered to a wall comes only from the velocity component normal to it: \( P=\rho\overline{v_x^2} \).

For random motion \( \overline{v_x^2}=\overline{v_y^2}=\overline{v_z^2}=\dfrac13\overline{v^2} \).

So \( P=\dfrac13\rho\overline{v^2} \).
questions.hint: Only one of the three perpendicular velocity components pushes on any given wall.
distractor_logic: Borrows the one-half from the kinetic-energy formula; the one-third comes from sharing among three directions
Drops the fraction, as if every molecule moved straight at the wall
Multiplies by 3 instead of dividing; only one of the three velocity components presses on a given wall

questions.topic: Pressure of an Ideal Gas and the Kinetic Interpretation of Temperature
questions.question: The factor \( \dfrac13 \) in the kinetic-theory pressure formula arises because
options: kinetic energy is averaged over three stages of each collision
only the velocity component perpendicular to a given wall transfers momentum to it, and on average this is one-third of \( \overline{v^2} \)
only one-third of the molecules are moving towards any given wall
two-thirds of the momentum is lost in each wall collision
questions.explanation:
A molecule hitting a wall normal to \( x \) transfers \( 2mv_x \), which leads to \( P=nm\overline{v_x^2} \).

Random motion makes the three directions equivalent: \( \overline{v^2}=\overline{v_x^2}+\overline{v_y^2}+\overline{v_z^2}=3\overline{v_x^2} \).

Hence the \( \dfrac13 \): it is a geometric sharing among three perpendicular directions.
questions.hint: Write \( \overline{v^2} \) as the sum of its three components and ask which one matters for one wall.
distractor_logic: No energy averaging over collision stages occurs in the derivation; the factor is geometric, not energetic
All molecules contribute; the factor comes from splitting the mean square speed among three directions, not from counting molecules
Collisions are perfectly elastic, so no momentum or energy is lost

questions.topic: Pressure of an Ideal Gas and the Kinetic Interpretation of Temperature
questions.question: The average translational kinetic energy of a molecule of an ideal gas at absolute temperature \( T \) is
questions.explanation:
Combining \( P=\dfrac13nm\overline{v^2} \) with \( P=nk_BT \) gives \( \dfrac13m\overline{v^2}=k_BT \).

So \( \dfrac12m\overline{v^2}=\dfrac32k_BT \).
questions.hint: Three translational directions, each contributing equally.
distractor_logic: This is the share of only one translational direction, not all three
Doubles the correct value by dropping the one-half of kinetic energy
Uses the molar constant \( R \); \( \dfrac32RT \) is the energy of a whole mole, not one molecule

questions.topic: Pressure of an Ideal Gas and the Kinetic Interpretation of Temperature
questions.question: The absolute temperature of an ideal gas is doubled. The average translational kinetic energy of its molecules
questions.explanation:
Average translational KE \( =\dfrac32k_BT \), directly proportional to \( T \).

Doubling \( T \) doubles it. (It is the speed, not the energy, that scales as \( \sqrt T \).)
questions.hint: Look at how \( T \) appears in \( \dfrac32k_BT \).
distractor_logic: Squares the temperature ratio; kinetic energy is proportional to \( T \), not \( T^2 \)
Applies the square-root dependence that belongs to molecular speed, not to energy
Ignores that average kinetic energy is set directly by temperature

questions.topic: Pressure of an Ideal Gas and the Kinetic Interpretation of Temperature
questions.question: Helium and oxygen are kept at the same temperature. Compared with an oxygen molecule, a helium molecule has
options: the same average translational kinetic energy
a larger average translational kinetic energy because it is lighter
a smaller average translational kinetic energy because it is lighter
questions.explanation:
Average translational KE per molecule is \( \dfrac32k_BT \), which contains no mass.

At the same \( T \) both gases have equal average translational KE; the lighter helium molecule simply moves faster.
questions.hint: Does the expression for average kinetic energy contain the molecular mass?
distractor_logic: Lighter molecules move faster, but the kinetic energy works out equal at equal \( T \)
The lower mass is exactly compensated by a higher speed; average kinetic energy depends on \( T \) alone
Equal kinetic energy with unequal masses means unequal speeds; helium is faster

questions.topic: Pressure of an Ideal Gas and the Kinetic Interpretation of Temperature
questions.question: The pressure of an ideal gas equals what fraction of its total translational kinetic energy per unit volume?
questions.explanation:
\( P=\dfrac13\rho\overline{v^2} \) and kinetic energy per unit volume \( \dfrac EV=\dfrac12\rho\overline{v^2} \).

\( \dfrac{P}{E/V}=\dfrac{1/3}{1/2}=\dfrac23 \), so \( P=\dfrac23\dfrac EV \).
questions.hint: Divide \( \dfrac13\rho\overline{v^2} \) by \( \dfrac12\rho\overline{v^2} \).
distractor_logic: Takes the one-third from \( P=\dfrac13\rho\overline{v^2} \) but forgets that energy per volume is \( \dfrac12\rho\overline{v^2} \)
Uses the one-half from the kinetic-energy formula as the whole answer
Inverts the ratio; energy per unit volume is larger than the pressure

questions.topic: Pressure of an Ideal Gas and the Kinetic Interpretation of Temperature
questions.question: According to the classical kinetic theory of an ideal gas, the average translational kinetic energy of the molecules at 0 K would be
options: the same as at room temperature
questions.explanation:
Classically, average translational KE \( =\dfrac32k_BT \).

At \( T=0 \) K this is zero: molecular motion would stop. This is why absolute zero is the natural zero of the kinetic temperature scale.
questions.hint: Substitute \( T=0 \) in the expression for average kinetic energy.
distractor_logic: Reverses the trend; kinetic energy grows with \( T \), so it is smallest at 0 K
Treats \( T \) as 1 in \( \dfrac32k_BT \); at \( T=0 \) the product is zero
Ignores that kinetic energy is proportional to absolute temperature

questions.topic: Pressure of an Ideal Gas and the Kinetic Interpretation of Temperature
questions.question: The total translational kinetic energy of one mole of an ideal gas at temperature \( T \) is
questions.explanation:
Each molecule has \( \dfrac32k_BT \); a mole has \( N_A \) molecules.

\( E=N_A\times\dfrac32k_BT=\dfrac32RT \), since \( N_Ak_B=R \).
questions.hint: Multiply the per-molecule value by Avogadro's number.
distractor_logic: Gives the energy of a single molecule, not of a mole
Counts only one of the three translational directions
Doubles the correct value by dropping the one-half of kinetic energy

questions.topic: RMS Speed, Average Speed, and Most Probable Speed of Gas Molecules
questions.question: The root-mean-square speed of the molecules of a gas of molar mass \( M \) at temperature \( T \) is
questions.explanation:
From \( \dfrac12mv_{rms}^2=\dfrac32k_BT \): \( v_{rms}=\sqrt{\dfrac{3k_BT}{m}} \).

Multiplying numerator and denominator by \( N_A \) (with \( N_Ak_B=R \) and \( N_Am=M \)) gives \( v_{rms}=\sqrt{\dfrac{3RT}{M}} \).
questions.hint: The rms speed comes straight from \( \dfrac12mv_{rms}^2=\dfrac32k_BT \).
distractor_logic: The coefficient 2 belongs to the most probable speed
The coefficient \( \dfrac8\pi \) belongs to the average speed
Pairs \( R \) with the single-molecule mass \( m \); \( R \) must go with the molar mass \( M \)

The coefficients inside the square roots are \( 2 \), \( \dfrac8\pi\approx2.55 \) and \( 3 \).

So \( v_{mp}:v_{avg}:v_{rms}=\sqrt2:\sqrt{8/\pi}:\sqrt3\approx1.41:1.60:1.73 \), giving \( v_{mp}

questions.topic: RMS Speed, Average Speed, and Most Probable Speed of Gas Molecules
questions.question: The most probable speed of gas molecules of mass \( m \) at temperature \( T \) is
questions.explanation:
The three characteristic speeds differ only in their coefficient: 2 for \( v_{mp} \), \( \dfrac8\pi \) for \( v_{avg} \), 3 for \( v_{rms} \).

With per-molecule quantities, \( v_{mp}=\sqrt{\dfrac{2k_BT}{m}} \).
questions.hint: The most probable speed has the smallest coefficient of the three.
distractor_logic: The coefficient 3 belongs to the rms speed
The coefficient \( \dfrac8\pi \) belongs to the average speed

questions.topic: RMS Speed, Average Speed, and Most Probable Speed of Gas Molecules
questions.question: The absolute temperature of a gas is made four times larger. The root-mean-square speed of its molecules becomes
questions.explanation:
\( v_{rms}=\sqrt{\dfrac{3RT}{M}}\propto\sqrt T \).

\( \sqrt4=2 \), so \( v_{rms} \) doubles.
questions.hint: Speed goes as the square root of absolute temperature.
distractor_logic: Treats speed as proportional to \( T \); it is energy that scales with \( T \)

questions.topic: RMS Speed, Average Speed, and Most Probable Speed of Gas Molecules
questions.question: At 300 K, which of these gases has the greatest root-mean-square speed?
questions.explanation:
At equal \( T \), \( v_{rms}=\sqrt{\dfrac{3RT}{M}}\propto\dfrac{1}{\sqrt M} \).

Molar masses: \( H_2 \) 2, He 4, \( N_2 \) 28, \( O_2 \) 32 g/mol. The lightest, \( H_2 \), is fastest.
questions.hint: At the same temperature, lighter molecules move faster.
distractor_logic: Oxygen has the heaviest molecules here, so it is actually the slowest

questions.topic: RMS Speed, Average Speed, and Most Probable Speed of Gas Molecules
questions.question: On the Maxwell speed-distribution curve of a gas, the speed at which the curve reaches its peak is
options: the maximum speed any molecule can have
questions.explanation:
The peak marks the speed shared by the largest fraction of molecules, which by definition is \( v_{mp} \).

Because the curve has a long high-speed tail, \( v_{avg} \) and \( v_{rms} \) both lie to the right of the peak, in the order \( v_{mp}
questions.hint: Which speed do the largest number of molecules have?
distractor_logic: The rms speed lies to the right of the peak
The average speed also lies to the right of the peak, though closer than the rms speed

questions.topic: RMS Speed, Average Speed, and Most Probable Speed of Gas Molecules
questions.question: When the temperature of a gas is increased, its Maxwell speed-distribution curve
options: shifts its peak to a lower speed and becomes taller
keeps its peak at the same speed but becomes narrower
shifts its peak to a higher speed and becomes flatter and broader
shifts its peak to a higher speed and becomes taller
questions.explanation:
\( v_{mp}=\sqrt{\dfrac{2RT}{M}} \) rises with \( T \), so the peak moves right.

The area under the curve equals the total number of molecules, which is unchanged, so as the curve spreads over more speeds its peak must drop.
questions.hint: The area under the curve counts the molecules and cannot change.
distractor_logic: Reverses both effects; heating speeds molecules up
Heating changes the most probable speed, which grows as \( \sqrt T \)
The area under the curve (number of molecules) is fixed, so a broader curve must be lower, not taller

questions.topic: RMS Speed, Average Speed, and Most Probable Speed of Gas Molecules
questions.question: The average speed of the molecules of a gas of molar mass \( M \) at temperature \( T \) is
questions.explanation:
The average speed carries the coefficient \( \dfrac8\pi \): \( v_{avg}=\sqrt{\dfrac{8RT}{\pi M}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{8k_BT}{\pi m}} \).

Since \( 2<\dfrac8\pi<3 \), it lies between \( v_{mp} \) and \( v_{rms} \).
questions.hint: The average speed has \( \pi \) in its formula.
distractor_logic: Drops the \( \pi \) in the denominator, which would make it larger than even the rms speed
The coefficient 3 belongs to the rms speed

questions.topic: Degrees of Freedom and the Law of Equipartition of Energy
questions.question: The number of degrees of freedom \( f \) of a molecule of a monatomic gas such as helium is
questions.explanation:
A monatomic molecule behaves as a point: it can only translate along \( x \), \( y \) and \( z \).

Rotation of a point carries negligible energy, so \( f=3 \).
questions.hint: Count the independent directions in which a point particle can move.
distractor_logic: 5 applies to a rigid diatomic molecule, which can also rotate
6 applies to a non-linear polyatomic molecule with three rotations
A point atom still moves in three independent directions, not one

questions.topic: Degrees of Freedom and the Law of Equipartition of Energy
questions.question: A rigid diatomic molecule such as \( O_2 \) at ordinary temperatures has how many degrees of freedom?
questions.explanation:
Translation: 3. Rotation: 2, about the two axes perpendicular to the bond.

Rotation about the bond axis has negligible moment of inertia, and a rigid molecule does not vibrate, so \( f=3+2=5 \).
questions.hint: Add the translational and rotational counts; a rigid molecule does not vibrate.
distractor_logic: Counts translation only and ignores the two rotations
Adds a third rotation about the molecular axis, which carries negligible energy
Includes vibration, which a rigid molecule does not have

questions.topic: Degrees of Freedom and the Law of Equipartition of Energy
questions.question: The law of equipartition of energy states that, in thermal equilibrium at temperature \( T \), each degree of freedom of a molecule has an average energy of
questions.explanation:
Each independent quadratic energy term (a degree of freedom) receives \( \dfrac12k_BT \) per molecule, or \( \dfrac12RT \) per mole.

Three translational terms give the familiar \( \dfrac32k_BT \).
questions.hint: Three translational degrees together give \( \dfrac32k_BT \). What does each one get?
distractor_logic: Double the correct share; \( k_BT \) belongs to a whole vibrational mode, which has two energy terms
\( \dfrac32k_BT \) is the total translational energy for all three directions
Uses the molar constant \( R \) for a single molecule

questions.topic: Degrees of Freedom and the Law of Equipartition of Energy
questions.question: Why does a diatomic molecule have only 2 rotational degrees of freedom, not 3?
options: Collisions prevent rotation about the third axis
A diatomic molecule can rotate about only one axis
The two atoms repel each other when rotating about the bond axis
Its moment of inertia about the bond axis is negligible, so rotation about that axis carries negligible energy
questions.explanation:
Both atoms lie on the bond axis and act as point masses on that line.

The moment of inertia about the bond axis is therefore negligible, and so is the rotational energy about it. Only the two perpendicular axes count.
questions.hint: Think about where the mass of the molecule lies relative to the bond axis.
distractor_logic: Collisions do not forbid any rotation; the issue is the negligible moment of inertia
It rotates about two perpendicular axes, not one
Repulsion is not the reason; the atoms lie on the axis, so the moment of inertia about it is almost zero

questions.explanation:

questions.question: How many translational degrees of freedom does a \( CO_2 \) molecule have?
questions.explanation:
Every molecule, whatever its shape, can move its centre of mass independently along \( x \), \( y \) and \( z \).

So translational degrees of freedom are always 3; shape affects only the rotational count.

questions.question: For one mole of an ideal gas, the molar specific heats at constant pressure and at constant volume are related by
questions.explanation:
At constant pressure, extra heat is needed for the work \( P\Delta V=R\Delta T \) per mole.

So \( C_p=C_v+R \), i.e. \( C_p-C_v=R \) (Mayer's relation).

questions.explanation:
A monatomic molecule has only 3 translational degrees of freedom, so \( U=\dfrac32RT \) per mole.

questions.topic: Specific Heat Capacities of Gases and Mean Free Path
questions.question: The mean free path of a gas molecule is
options: the average distance it travels between two successive collisions
the average distance between neighbouring molecules
the average distance of a molecule from the nearest wall
questions.explanation:
Between collisions a molecule moves in a straight line.

The mean free path \( \lambda \) is the average length of these straight segments, i.e. the average distance between successive collisions.
questions.hint: The word 'free' refers to motion without collisions.
distractor_logic: The spacing between neighbours is much smaller than the free path in a gas
The diameter sets the collision cross-section but is not the distance travelled

questions.topic: Specific Heat Capacities of Gases and Mean Free Path
questions.question: The mean free path of molecules of diameter \( d \) in a gas of number density \( n \) is
questions.explanation:
A molecule sweeps out a collision cylinder of cross-section \( \pi d^2 \), which would give \( \dfrac{1}{\pi d^2n} \) if the others stood still.

All molecules move, and the average relative speed is \( \sqrt2 \) times the average speed, so this is divided by \( \sqrt2 \): \( \lambda=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2\,\pi d^2n} \).
questions.hint: The cross-section is an area, and moving targets make collisions more frequent.
distractor_logic: Drops the \( \sqrt2 \) correction for the relative motion of the molecules
Puts \( \sqrt2 \) in the numerator; relative motion shortens the free path, it does not lengthen it

questions.question: At constant temperature, the pressure of a gas is increased. Its mean free path
options: rises at first and then falls
questions.explanation:
\( \lambda=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2\,\pi d^2n} \) and \( n=\dfrac{P}{k_BT} \).

At fixed \( T \), raising \( P \) raises \( n \), so \( \lambda\propto\dfrac1P \) decreases.
questions.hint: How does number density change with pressure at fixed temperature?

Ignores that \( n=\dfrac{P}{k_BT} \) rises with pressure

questions.question: If the molecular diameter were doubled, with number density unchanged, the mean free path would become
questions.explanation:
\( \lambda=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2\,\pi d^2n} \); with \( n \) fixed, \( \lambda\propto\dfrac{1}{d^2} \).

Doubling \( d \) multiplies \( d^2 \) by 4, so \( \lambda \) becomes \( \dfrac14 \) of its value.
questions.hint: \( \lambda \) depends on the square of the diameter, in the denominator.
distractor_logic: Uses \( d \) instead of \( d^2 \)
Makes \( \lambda \) grow with molecular size
Squares correctly but inverts the dependence

questions.explanation:
For a fixed amount, \( \dfrac{PV}{T} \) is constant, so \( T\propto PV \).

\( PV \) becomes \( 2\times3=6 \) times larger.

\( T_2=6\times300=1800 \) K.

questions.question: An ideal gas of molar mass \( M \) is at pressure \( P \) and temperature \( T \). Its density \( \rho \) is
questions.explanation:
Write \( \mu=\dfrac{w}{M} \) for a sample of mass \( w \) in \( PV=\mu RT \): \( PV=\dfrac wMRT \).

Density \( \rho=\dfrac wV=\dfrac{PM}{RT} \).

The per-molecule version is \( \rho=\dfrac{Pm}{k_BT} \); mixing \( m \) with \( R \) is dimensionally wrong.

questions.explanation:

\( V=\dfrac{300}{10^{4}}=3\times10^{-2} \) m\( ^3 \), i.e. 30 litres.

questions.question: 2 mol of gas A and 3 mol of gas B are mixed in a closed container, and the total pressure is \( 5\times10^{5} \) Pa. Treating both as ideal and non-reacting, the partial pressure of gas A is
questions.explanation:
Each gas behaves as if alone: \( P_A=\dfrac{\mu_ART}{V} \), so partial pressure is proportional to the number of moles.

\( P_A=\dfrac25\times5\times10^{5}=2\times10^{5} \) Pa.

questions.topic: Kinetic Theory Postulates and the Ideal Gas Equation
questions.question: Two containers of equal volume, at the same temperature and pressure, hold hydrogen and oxygen respectively. Which statement is correct?
options: The oxygen container holds 16 times as many molecules
Both contain the same number of molecules
The hydrogen container holds 16 times as many molecules
Both contain the same mass of gas
questions.explanation:
From \( PV=Nk_BT \), \( N=\dfrac{PV}{k_BT} \), which contains no molecular mass.

Equal \( P \), \( V \) and \( T \) therefore mean equal \( N \) (Avogadro's hypothesis), while the masses differ in the ratio of molar masses.
questions.hint: Does molecular mass appear in \( PV=Nk_BT \)?

questions.question: At constant pressure, an ideal gas occupying 2 L at 300 K is heated to 450 K. Its new volume is
questions.explanation:
At constant \( P \), \( V\propto T \) (Charles's law, from \( PV=\mu RT \)).

\( V_2=2\times\dfrac{450}{300}=3 \) L.
questions.hint: At constant pressure, volume is proportional to absolute temperature.

questions.question: A real gas behaves most like an ideal gas at
questions.explanation:
Kinetic theory assumes negligible molecular volume and negligible attractions.

Low pressure spreads the molecules far apart, so their size hardly matters.

High temperature makes them fast, so brief attractions hardly matter. Both assumptions hold best together.

questions.question: A closed container of gas is on a train that starts moving steadily at high speed. Compared with when the train was at rest, the temperature of the gas

falls, because the molecules lag behind the moving container
rises in proportion to the square of the train's speed
is unchanged, because temperature depends only on random motion relative to the container
